plan.title: bug(hooks): a write to a target outside every worktree is gated by the payload root's occupancy lease

narratives.Description: bug(hooks): a write to a target outside every worktree is gated by the payload root's occupancy lease
narratives.Overview:
## Summary

A write whose target lies outside every worktree is gated by the **payload root's** occupancy lease. `admitEffectiveHookRoot` returns `admitPayload(payload, null)` when the target has no resolvable worktree, so a destination belonging to no repository -- a path under `%TEMP%`, a home-directory file, anything outside a checkout -- inherits the payload root's occupancy and ritual state. The lease then serialises writes anywhere the agent touches, not only inside the checkout it describes.

Split from #3954 section 3 on the accepted set-level design-critique arc (successor lean https://github.com/deftai/directive/issues/3954#issuecomment-5480338725, completed-arc record 5480360433). Accepted finding 11 of 24: this is neither an identity nor a lifecycle question, it shares no remedy surface with the actor split or with lease release, and holding it inside #3954 made that issue un-landable as one unit.

## Measured at `fb9ece05`

- `packages/core/src/hooks/dispatcher.ts:626-636` has three fallbacks to the payload root: a null write target, no existing ancestor directory, and no worktree for that ancestor. The third is the one that fires for ordinary non-repository destinations.
- Observed live on 2026-08-31T08:15Z: a write to a path under `%TEMP%` was denied naming the primary checkout's occupant (`Directive denied write: Worktree occupied by session host:claude:v1:...`), while the checkout itself was not the target.
- **Not relieved or worsened by #3987.** `isInRepoShellWritePath` (`packages/core/src/hooks/shell-write-targets.ts:240-249`) returns false for any destination resolving outside the project root, so the landed shell-write classifier does not extend payload-root gating to out-of-tree shell writes. The fallback fires on the direct-write and MCP surfaces, before and after the rest of #3987 lands.
- Scale: with 100+ worktrees under `.deft-scratch/worktrees/`, the coupling widens as cohort size grows -- one lease can serialise unrelated scratch writes across a whole cohort.

## Why this is its own issue

The remedy surface is root resolution, not actor resolution. Nothing about who the actor is, or when a lease is released, decides whether a target outside every worktree should inherit the payload root's lease at all. The #3954 arc kept the two actor-resolution sections and the lease-lifecycle work together and split this out for that reason.

## Candidate remedies, not prescribed

1. `effectiveRoot` declines to fall back when the target lies outside every worktree: no root, no gating.
2. Keep the gating but narrow it -- admit an out-of-tree target when the payload root's lease is held by the presenting session, and refuse only the in-tree foreign-lease case.
3. Publish the fallback as deliberate, with the reason stated, and keep the current behaviour.

They differ in what they protect: 1 and 2 stop a lease from reaching outside its checkout, 3 accepts that reach and makes it discoverable. Note the #3794 rationale already distinguishes "no containment question exists" from "a question asked and left unanswered"; whichever remedy is chosen has to say which of those an out-of-tree target is.

## Acceptance criteria

1. A write whose target lies outside every worktree is either not gated by the payload root's lease, or the fallback is published as deliberate with its reason.
2. In-tree behaviour and the #3794 foreign-worktree refusals are unchanged, with tests.
3. A regression test covers an out-of-tree target while a live foreign lease is held on the payload root.
4. The decision records whether the direct-write and MCP surfaces differ.

## Design-critique

`mechanism-shaped: true`

The remedy space is open and this changes gate semantics for every host, so it takes its own arc before ingest. The #3954 arc critiqued the set it was split from, not this remedy space.

Refs #3954, #3794, #3987, #3433, #3755.

### Comment by @MScottAdams (2026-08-31T16:12:16Z)

model: gpt-5.6-sol
role: critic

Honored input ceiling: issue comment `5480978842` inclusive. Measured checkout: `fb9ece05` on `master`.

## Verdict

The refutation target does not survive. The current fallback is deliberate compatibility/containment behavior, not an accidental branch: #3794 explicitly required fallback to `payloadRoot` when a target worktree could not be admitted. That does not prove the policy is still desirable, but it changes this from “fix a defect” to “change the authority contract.” Neither narrowing remedy is safe as filed because the fallback selects more than a lease and because `admitMutationTargetSet` needs one root for the whole mutation.

What would flip this verdict on the filed target: evidence that out-of-tree direct writes are intended to bypass ritual, UAT/authz, runtime authority, and the intent ceiling—not merely occupancy—plus a closed mixed-target rule that preserves every #3794 refusal. A recut that names retained gates, canonicalizes targets, and proves the direct-write/Shell/MCP matrix would create a viable successor design, but would not make the filed premise true.

## Re-verification

I ran `npx vitest run packages/core/src/hooks/dispatcher-effective-root.test.ts --reporter=dot`: 27/27 tests passed. I also probed the built modules under `packages/core/dist` with real temporary repositories, linked worktrees, a foreign repository, nonexistent descendants, Windows junctions, mixed target sets, a foreign live lease, and direct-write versus prefixed-MCP tool names. No repository file was changed.

## blocks-the-design — #3794 deliberately preserved this fallback

**Evidence.** The original #3794 acceptance text says an `effectiveRoot` is admitted only when the common dirs match and “otherwise fall back to `payloadRoot`.” Commit `c99f6159` describes lookup failure as fallback; follow-up `bcd9d34e` split a *resolved other toplevel with unreadable identity* from the compatibility fallback. Current `dispatcher.ts:631-648` implements that split: no Git toplevel (`candidateRaw === null`) returns `admitPayload(payload, null)`, while a distinct candidate whose common dir cannot be read returns `unproven-identity`. My built-module probe reproduced those distinct outcomes.

**Failure mode.** The filed “defect” premise treats an intentionally preserved pre-#3794 behavior as accidental, then uses the rationale’s “question asked and left unanswered” language for a case the implementation represents as “no candidate Git toplevel.” That can drive a security-sensitive authority change without first replacing the compatibility invariant #3794 recorded.

**Disposition consequence.** Do not bind remedies 1 or 2 as bug fixes. Reframe this as an explicit policy change for the fourth case—payload is a repository, target has an existing ancestor, but that ancestor has no Git toplevel—and either retain/publish it or define the replacement authority contract.

## blocks-the-design — “no root, no gating” removes unrelated authority checks

**Evidence.** `inspectMutationGates` documents the split at `dispatcher.ts:1183-1187`. `effectiveRoot` drives occupancy and ritual (`:1255-1447`), scope inspection (`:1550-1634`), and the story-fence/assist-scratch path basis (`:1218-1238`, `:1645-1661`). Payload root remains authoritative for authz/UAT and its audit (`:1183-1187`, `:381-417`), project runtime-authority policy (`:803-840`), and the kill-switch. The intent ceiling runs independently at `:1637-1643`. For a true outside-root target, active scope is already inspected but its deny is deliberately skipped by #2885 at `:1563-1576`; ritual, authz/UAT, runtime authority, and intent still run. Thus the filed lease framing omits the checks whose behavior would have to be preserved.

**Failure mode.** A literal remedy 1 implementation that exits when there is “no root” lets an unritualed explore/triage session—or an agent acting on an injected absolute path—write a home/config/temp target without the mutation intent ceiling, UAT grant scope, or an enabled runtime deny-path policy. Removing active-scope friction buys nothing because outside-root writes already have that exemption.

**Disposition consequence.** Strike “no root, no gating.” If the desired change is lease isolation, introduce an explicit no-toplevel target class and state each gate’s disposition. At minimum, payload-root authz/UAT, project runtime policy, the intent ceiling, read-only posture, and kill-switch must remain independently evaluated unless this issue expressly changes them.

## blocks-the-design — occupancy cannot be bypassed without deciding ritual ownership

**Evidence.** #3794 records occupancy and ritual as one atomic seam, and current code cross-checks the admitted lease owner/member against `ritual.boundSessionId` at `dispatcher.ts:1388-1425` and again at `:1486-1506`. An out-of-tree direct write currently reads both from payload root. A matching presenter is already admitted; my foreign-lease probe denied `occupancy-occupied` before mutation. The same path also refreshes the payload lease immediately before an allowed write (`:1450-1509`).

**Failure mode.** Remedy 2 is not a complete state transition. If it bypasses only the foreign-lease refusal, either the presenter remains blocked by the ritual-owner mismatch, or the implementation suppresses that comparison and lets the presenter ride another session’s ritual ceremony. If it leaves the final recheck unchanged, the write still denies; if it refreshes unchanged, an unrelated out-of-tree write renews the payload lease the remedy was meant to decouple.

**Disposition consequence.** Specify whether no-toplevel direct writes require a fresh ritual, whose exact identity may satisfy it, and whether they may refresh any worktree lease. Add matching-owner, foreign-owner, granted-member, stale/missing ritual, and final-recheck cases. Until then remedy 2 is not buildable as a safe narrowing.

## blocks-the-design — a nullable root has no defined multi-target algebra

**Evidence.** `admitMutationTargetSet` admits every ApplyPatch member, then requires one unique root (`dispatcher.ts:657-683`). In my probe, `{primary target, outside target}` collapsed to primary and was admitted; `{linked-worktree target, outside target}` produced `worktree-span`; a foreign-repository member was refused before any later gate. Those outcomes come from the outside target currently contributing payload root to the set.

**Failure mode.** If remedy 1 makes the outside member contribute no root, a patch combining a linked-worktree product mutation with an injected absolute home/temp mutation can accidentally collapse to the linked root and evade the existing span refusal. If “no root” dominates instead, one outside member can suppress all gates for an in-tree product mutation. In a swarm, an untrusted ApplyPatch path is therefore an authority-selection input, exactly the injection/containment risk #3794 closed.

**Disposition consequence.** Define a target-class lattice before changing the return type: same admitted worktree; same-repository other worktree; foreign repository; unproven repository identity; and proven no-toplevel. State the combining result for every mixed set. Preserve `foreign-repository`, `unproven-identity`, and `worktree-span` refusal before any no-toplevel exemption.

## sharpens-framing — direct-write, Shell, and MCP are three different surfaces

**Evidence.** `tools.ts:1-16` classifies bare `search_replace` as a direct-write tool. A server-prefixed `tasks__search_replace` is MCP but not direct-write; `decideHook` routes MCP only through push/merge runtime classification at `dispatcher.ts:2301-2306`. My built probe gave the outside bare direct write `occupancy-occupied`, while the prefixed MCP spelling returned `shell-op-unclassifiable` and never consulted root admission. Shell is different again: #3987’s `isInRepoShellWritePath` rejects outside destinations (`shell-write-targets.ts:240-249`), so `decideShellWriteReissue` skips them (`dispatcher.ts:1750-1783`).

**Failure mode.** The body’s claim that the fallback fires on “direct-write and MCP surfaces” is false for generic prefixed MCP tools. Treating transport as authority class can either overclaim coverage or accidentally widen this issue into the separate question of mutation-capable MCP reachability. It also omits Shell, the measured surface that intentionally differs.

**Disposition consequence.** Replace AC4 with a required matrix: direct-write names, recognized Shell write forms, generic MCP, and any explicitly catalogued MCP mutation name. Decide whether generic MCP mutation gating is a separate issue; do not imply this root change covers it.

## sharpens-framing — target canonicalization must precede the new classification

**Evidence.** `existingAncestorDir` resolves `targetPath` against the dispatcher process cwd (`session/git.ts:174-193`), not against payload root or a host-supplied cwd. My probe passed payload root in a temp repo but a relative `src/a.ts` while the process cwd was this checkout; admission resolved this checkout as a foreign repository. A nonexistent descendant correctly inherited its nearest existing ancestor. Windows junction probes followed a junction into a linked worktree and admitted that worktree, while a junction into a non-repository directory fell back to payload root.

**Failure mode.** A rule written as “outside every worktree” is unstable until relative paths have one base. The same lexical target can be foreign, linked, or no-toplevel depending on hook process cwd. Symlink/junction and nonexistent-path behavior can likewise change which class reaches the exemption.

**Disposition consequence.** Add an AC that canonicalizes a target against the payload/host execution contract before `existingAncestorDir`, then tests absolute and relative targets, nonexistent descendants, junction/symlink targets, same-repo worktrees, and unrelated repos. The unrelated-repo and unreadable-identity refusals must remain prior to any exemption.

## sharpens-framing — the acceptance criteria neither pin the surviving gates nor define publication

**Evidence.** AC2 says only “in-tree behaviour” and foreign-worktree refusals are unchanged; AC3 exercises only a foreign payload lease. Neither observes ritual freshness, exact ritual owner, UAT/authz, runtime deny paths, intent ceiling, read-only posture, mixed ApplyPatch members, or lease refresh. AC1 permits “published as deliberate” without naming a publication surface. The #3794 issue and commits already record deliberate fallback, while the current source comment does not explain the no-toplevel case specifically.

**Failure mode.** A patch can satisfy AC3 by bypassing the whole mutation pipeline, which is precisely the unsafe implementation. Conversely, candidate 3 may be declared complete by citing old issue history even though no current operator-facing contract became more discoverable.

**Disposition consequence.** Expand acceptance to a gate-by-gate allow/deny matrix and mixed-target tests. For candidate 3, name the durable surface and required reason; otherwise that branch is either already satisfied historically or not objectively buildable.

## footnote — existing low-ceremony mechanisms narrow the need

Contained assist writes under `.deft-scratch/` or `temp/` already use the allowlist at `dispatcher.ts:420-438` and skip occupancy, ritual, and active scope while retaining authz and runtime policy. Out-of-tree active-scope writes already use #2885, and recognized outside Shell writes are not reissued into mutation gates. These do not settle arbitrary direct writes to home or OS temp, but they are the existing mechanisms a replacement should compose with rather than duplicate.

## Road not taken and steelman

The strongest case for narrowing is real: a worktree lease is a cooperative serialization primitive for that tree, so a foreign holder should not block an unrelated OS-temp note. A narrowly typed “no Git toplevel” result could bypass lease contention without touching proven foreign repositories. I rejected remedies 1 and 2 only because they do not preserve the rest of the authority stack or define mixed sets. The safest present choice is remedy 3 with an explicit reason, followed by a recut for an occupancy-only policy change if the broader matrix is intended.

The payload-root fallback for a target with no Git toplevel is **deliberate** compatibility behaviour that #3794 preserved on purpose, so this issue is a change to the authority contract rather than a defect fix -- and neither narrowing remedy is safe as filed, because the fallback selects more than a lease and `admitMutationTargetSet` needs one root for the whole mutation. ## In plain English

**I filed this as a bug. It is not one, and the critic showed that from the commit history and the code.**

- **The fallback is intended.** #3794's acceptance text required falling back to the payload root when a target worktree could not be admitted, and a follow-up commit deliberately *split* two cases: a target that resolves to another toplevel whose identity cannot be read fails closed as `unproven-identity`, while a target with no Git toplevel at all keeps the old payload-root behaviour. I re-derived that split in the current code. My filing used the rationale's "a question asked and left unanswered" language for the case the implementation represents as "no candidate toplevel" -- the other branch. So the premise the issue rests on is wrong.
- **"No root, no gating" would remove far more than a lease.** The effective root governs occupancy, ritual, active scope and the write fence; the payload root stays authoritative for authz and UAT grant scoping, the audit trail, the kill-switch and the outside-root carve-out, and the intent ceiling runs independently. My filing framed this as a lease problem. Remedy 1 taken literally would let an unritualed session -- or an agent acting on an injected absolute path -- write a home, config or temp target with no mutation intent ceiling and no UAT scope. And it buys nothing on active scope, because outside-root writes are already exempt there.
- **Remedy 2 is not a complete state transition.** Occupancy and ritual are cross-checked against each other: the admitted owner is compared with the ritual-bound session. Bypassing only the foreign-lease refusal either leaves the writer blocked by that comparison, or suppresses it and lets one session ride another's ceremony. The same path also refreshes the lease immediately before an allowed write, so an unrelated out-of-tree write would renew the very lease the remedy meant to decouple.
- **A nullable root has no defined behaviour for multi-target patches.** Target-set admission admits every member then demands one unique root. If an outside member contributes no root, a patch that mixes a linked-worktree edit with an injected absolute path can collapse to the linked root and evade the existing span refusal; if "no root" dominates instead, one outside member suppresses the gates for an in-tree edit. Untrusted patch paths become an authority-selection input, which is the containment risk #3794 closed.
- **My surface claim was false.** I wrote that the fallback fires on the direct-write and MCP surfaces. A generic server-prefixed MCP tool never consults root admission at all, and recognized shell writes to outside destinations are excluded by the landed #3987 classifier. Three surfaces, three behaviours.
- **"Outside every worktree" is not yet a stable rule.** Relative targets are resolved against the dispatcher process working directory, not the payload root, so the same lexical path can classify as foreign, linked or no-toplevel depending on where the hook runs. Junctions and nonexistent descendants shift the class too.
- **My acceptance criteria could be satisfied by the unsafe implementation.** They observe only a foreign lease, never ritual freshness or owner, authz, runtime policy, the intent ceiling, mixed patch members, or lease refresh -- and criterion 1 allows "published as deliberate" without naming where publication would live.

**What the synthesis would assert.** The safe landing is remedy 3: publish the no-toplevel case as deliberate on a durable operator-facing surface, with the reason stated and the surviving gates named gate by gate, plus target canonicalization and the three-surface matrix as acceptance. The narrowing remedies are not refused forever -- they are refused *as filed*, and a recut that names a target-class lattice (same admitted worktree, same-repository other worktree, foreign repository, unproven identity, proven no-toplevel), states the combining rule for every mixed set, and preserves the `foreign-repository`, `unproven-identity` and `worktree-span` refusals ahead of any exemption would be a viable successor design. It would still not make the filed premise true.

**What this arc does not do.** It implements nothing, opens no pull request, and does not close the issue. The friction I observed is real -- a foreign lease holder should not block an unrelated temp note -- but the record now says that costs an authority-contract change, not a bug fix.

**Disclosure.** I filed this issue, authored its measurements and its three remedies, wrote the write-back, and I am the synthesizer. I originated none of the seven findings, and four of them contradict my filing. The critic is a different family from mine and is not the seat whose finding produced this split.

## In plain English

**I filed this issue as a bug an hour ago. It is not a bug, and the critic showed that from the commit history and the code rather than by argument.**

10→The behaviour is deliberate. When a write target has no Git toplevel at all -- a path under the OS temp directory, a home-directory file -- the hook gates it against the payload root. #3794's own acceptance text required that fallback, and a later commit deliberately split it from a different case: a target that *does* resolve to another repository whose identity cannot be read fails closed instead. My filing quoted the rationale for the fail-closed branch and applied it to the fallback branch. That is the wrong half.

So the friction is real -- a foreign lease holder should not block an unrelated temp note -- but fixing it costs a change to the authority contract, not a bug fix. Three measured reasons the two narrowing remedies I proposed cannot land as written:

**The lease is not the only thing that fallback selects.** The effective root governs occupancy, ritual, active scope and the write fence. The payload root separately governs authz and UAT grant scoping, the audit trail and the kill-switch, and the mutation intent ceiling runs on its own. "No root, no gating" would drop those for out-of-tree writes, which means an unritualed session -- or an agent acting on an absolute path it read in an issue -- could write a home or config file with no intent ceiling and no grant scope. It also buys nothing on active scope, which already exempts outside-root writes.

**Bypassing the lease alone is not a complete state transition.** Occupancy and ritual are checked against each other: the admitted owner is compared with the session the ritual is bound to. Relax only the lease refusal and the writer is still blocked by that comparison -- or the implementation suppresses it and one session rides another's ceremony. The same path re-stamps the lease just before an allowed write, so an unrelated temp write would renew the lease the change was meant to decouple.

**A root that can be absent has no defined answer for multi-file patches.** Target-set admission admits every member and then demands one unique root. If an outside member contributes nothing, a patch mixing a linked-worktree edit with an injected absolute path can collapse to the linked root and evade the existing span refusal. If absence dominates instead, one outside member disables the gates for the in-tree edit beside it. Untrusted patch paths would become an authority-selection input, which is what #3794 closed.

20→Two smaller corrections to my filing. I claimed the fallback fires on the direct-write and MCP surfaces: a generic server-prefixed MCP tool never consults root admission at all, and recognized shell writes to outside destinations are already excluded, so there are three surfaces with three behaviours. And "outside every worktree" is not yet a stable rule, because a relative target is resolved against the process working directory rather than the payload root -- the same path can classify three different ways depending on where the hook runs.

**What this means for the work.** The landing this arc accepts is the third remedy: publish the no-toplevel case as deliberate on a durable operator-facing surface, state the reason, and name the gates that survive, gate by gate -- with target canonicalization and the three-surface matrix as acceptance rather than the lease-only criteria I wrote. The narrowing remedies are refused *as filed*, not forever: a recut that defines the target classes, states the combining rule for every mixed set, and keeps the foreign-repository, unproven-identity and span refusals ahead of any exemption would be a viable successor design. It would still not make the filed premise true.

**What this arc does not do.** It implements nothing, opens no pull request, and does not close the issue.

## Record

Charter refutation, spend N=1 -- panel permission was available on blast radius and deliberately not spent, because this issue is the narrow slice an N=3 panel split off an hour earlier. One critic post: 5481096005 (`gpt-5.6-sol`, ceiling 5480978842, measured at `fb9ece05`), 4 blocking, 3 sharpening, 1 footnote. The take map on 5481139589 is total over all seven classified headings, every take accept-into-contract, no residual, no audit marker open.

30→No round 2: nothing is contested, and the parent introduced no load-bearing premise while adjudicating. Five of the nine table rows are parent re-derivations, including a re-run of the effective-root suite (27 tests green).

Disclosure: the synthesizer filed this issue, authored its measurements and its three remedies, and posted the write-back. It originated none of the seven findings, and four of them contradict its filing. The critic is a different model family and is not the seat whose finding produced this split.

## Bookkeeping

items.title: Do not implement the issue body's remedies 1 or 2. The arc refused both as filed: the payload-root fallback for a target with no Git toplevel is deliberate behaviour #3794 preserved, so narrowing it is an authority-contract change rather than a defect fix.

Publish the no-toplevel case as deliberate on a durable operator-facing surface, with the reason stated. The current source comment explains the unproven-identity split but not the no-toplevel branch specifically; name the publication surface in the PR body rather than citing #3794 issue history as sufficient.

Name the surviving gates gate by gate for a no-toplevel target: occupancy and ritual resolve through the payload root; authz and UAT grant scoping, the authz audit trail, the kill-switch and `deny().projectRoot` stay payload-root authoritative; the mutation intent ceiling runs independently; active scope is inspected but its deny is skipped by #2885. State each disposition rather than describing the case as a lease question.

Record the three-surface matrix instead of the body's claim that the fallback fires on the direct-write and MCP surfaces: a bare direct-write name consults root admission, a generic server-prefixed MCP name does not reach it, and recognized shell writes to outside destinations are excluded by the landed #3987 classifier.

Lock the published behaviour with characterization tests: a no-toplevel direct-write target under a foreign payload-root lease, the same target with a matching presenter, the generic-MCP non-consultation, and the shell exclusion. Keep the existing effective-root suite green (27 tests at `fb9ece05`) and preserve the `foreign-repository`, `unproven-identity` and `worktree-span` refusals unchanged.

Record, do not fix here, that `existingAncestorDir` resolves a relative target against the dispatcher process working directory rather than the payload root, so the same lexical path can classify as foreign, linked or no-toplevel depending on where the hook runs. Canonicalization belongs to the successor recut; note it in the publication as a known limitation and open a follow-up issue for it.

Recorded as out of scope: any change to admission behaviour, the target-class lattice and mixed-set combining rule a narrowing would need, the #3954 actor work, #3999's release lifecycle, and #3987's bound remedy.
